title: Jeremiah 21:1–14
context: The narrator introduces a word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD when King Zedekiah sent Pashhur son of Malchijah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD, because Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was making war on Jerusalem. This Pashhur is distinguished from Pashhur son of Immer, the temple officer who struck Jeremiah in 20:1; Pashhur son of Malchijah appears again among the officials in 38:1. A similar but separate inquiry, sent by Zedekiah through Jehucal and the same Zephaniah, is reported in 37:3. Zedekiah hopes the LORD will act with wondrous works as in the past, but Jeremiah answers with the LORD’s word: the LORD himself will fight against the city, pestilence will strike, and Zedekiah and the survivors will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar (compare the fall of the city in Jeremiah 39 and 52 and 2 Kings 25). The LORD then sets before the people the way of life and the way of death: those who stay in the city will die, while those who go out and surrender to the Chaldeans will live (compare 38:2). This is a concrete offer during the siege, and it echoes the choice of Deuteronomy 30:15 and 30:19. The unit closes with a word to the house of David to execute justice each morning and a warning against those who trust in the city’s strong position. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage in its historical frame, as shared ground about God’s justice, his warnings, and the mercy of a way of escape even in judgment.

verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchijah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the narrator introducing a word from the LORD when King Zedekiah sent Pashhur son of Malchijah and Zephaniah to Jeremiah. The king turns to the prophet in crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the setting of the siege and the king’s request carefully introduced. Readers in both traditions commonly distinguish this Pashhur from the Pashhur of 20:1.

verses.text: “Please inquire of the LORD for us; for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon makes war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, that he may withdraw from us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Zedekiah’s envoys asking Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD, hoping for wondrous works that would make Nebuchadnezzar withdraw. The king hopes for rescue without repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king appealing to God’s past deeds while ignoring his present word. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against treating God as a resource only in emergencies.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to them, “Tell Zedekiah:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jeremiah answering the envoys with a message for Zedekiah. The prophet speaks what the LORD gives, not what the king wants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jeremiah faithfully delivering the LORD’s word to the king. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of prophetic courage before the powerful.

verses.text: ‘The LORD, the God of Israel says, “Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, with which you fight against the king of Babylon, and against the Chaldeans who besiege you outside the walls; and I will gather them into the middle of this city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will turn back the weapons of Judah’s defenders and gather the enemy into the city. The hoped-for rescue will not come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God reversing the king’s expectations. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the LORD’s sober announcement of judgment in its historical setting.

verses.text: I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, in wrath, and in great indignation.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he himself will fight against the city with an outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and wrath. The language of the exodus is turned against Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same exodus language (compare Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 4:34) now used of judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as God’s just response to long rebellion.

verses.text: I will strike the inhabitants of this city, both man and animal. They will die of a great pestilence.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD announcing that a great pestilence will strike the people and animals of the city. The siege brings terrible suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the severity of covenant judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse with sorrow, as a sober statement of what the siege will bring.

verses.text: Afterward,” says the LORD, “I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants, and the people, even those who are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life. He will strike them with the edge of the sword. He will not spare them, have pity, or have mercy.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that Zedekiah and the survivors will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar, who will not spare them. The king’s hopes end in captivity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word fulfilled in the fall of the city (compare Jeremiah 52:10–11; 2 Kings 25:7). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, without dwelling on its violence.

verses.text: “You shall say to this people, ‘The LORD says: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD setting before the people the way of life and the way of death. They hear a real choice offered during the siege, echoing Deuteronomy 30:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same echo of Deuteronomy and a genuine offer in the historical crisis. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its siege setting, as shared ground about God’s mercy offering escape.

verses.text: He who remains in this city will die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, but he who goes out and passes over to the Chaldeans who besiege you, he will live, and he will escape with his life.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that those who stay in the city will die, while those who surrender to the Chaldeans will live. The offer is concrete and practical.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same concrete offer, repeated in 38:2. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as a historical word about surrender during the siege, not a general statement about salvation.

verses.text: For I have set my face on this city for evil, and not for good,” says the LORD. “It will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he has set his face against the city for evil, so it will be burned by the king of Babylon. The city’s fate is settled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s determined judgment on Jerusalem. Both traditions commonly read the verse alongside the offer of escape, holding together judgment on the city and mercy to those who surrender.

verses.text: “Concerning the house of the king of Judah, hear the LORD’s word:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jeremiah calling the royal house of Judah to hear the LORD’s word. The king is accountable to God like everyone else.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the house of David addressed directly. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a call to justice in its historical setting.

verses.text: House of David, the LORD says, ‘Execute justice in the morning, and deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD calling the house of David to execute justice in the morning and rescue the robbed from the oppressor. Justice is urgent and daily.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s duty to protect the vulnerable (compare Psalm 72:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s demand for justice from rulers.

verses.text: Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, and of the rock of the plain,’ says the LORD. ‘You that say, “Who would come down against us?” or, “Who would enter into our homes?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD declaring himself against those who feel secure in their strong position and say no one can come against them. False security invites judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD confronting the city’s confidence in its walls and terrain. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against trusting human defenses.

verses.text: I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings,’ says the LORD; ‘and I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it will devour all that is around her.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will punish according to the fruit of their doings and kindle a fire in her forest. Judgment fits the deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God judging according to what people have done (compare Jeremiah 17:10). Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, within its historical frame.
